reference.source: Williams Hematology / WHO classification of haematolymphoid tumours
clinicalPearls: A systemic disorder in which misfolded monoclonal immunoglobulin light chains deposit as amyloid fibrils and damage organs
Cardiac involvement causes a restrictive cardiomyopathy with heart failure and is the main determinant of prognosis
Renal deposition typically produces heavy proteinuria and nephrotic syndrome, while other targets include the nerves, liver and soft tissues
Suggestive clinical clues include periorbital purpura, macroglossia, unexplained heart failure with preserved ejection fraction and non-diabetic nephrotic-range proteinuria
Tissue biopsy stained with Congo red shows amyloid with characteristic apple-green birefringence under polarised light
Confirming the amyloid is light-chain type, usually by mass spectrometry typing, is essential because treatment differs markedly from other amyloid types
An underlying clonal plasma cell population is identified with serum free light chain assay, electrophoresis and marrow examination, and management is plasma-cell-directed therapy
reference.pathophysiology: AL amyloidosis is driven by a clonal, usually small, population of bone marrow plasma cells that produce an unstable monoclonal immunoglobulin light chain. This light chain misfolds and aggregates into insoluble beta-pleated sheet amyloid fibrils that deposit in the extracellular space of vital organs. The fibrils disrupt tissue architecture, and circulating light chains also exert direct toxicity, particularly on cardiomyocytes. Progressive infiltration of the heart, kidneys, nerves, liver and soft tissues produces the multisystem clinical picture, and the amount and toxicity of the light chain, rather than tumour burden, drive organ damage.
additionalDifferentials: AA (serum amyloid A) amyloidosis from chronic inflammation
additionalInvestigations: Serum free light chain assay with serum and urine immunofixation
Congo red staining of an affected tissue or fat aspirate for apple-green birefringence
Amyloid typing by mass spectrometry or immunohistochemistry
Cardiac biomarkers (natriuretic peptides, troponin) and echocardiography or cardiac MRI
Bone marrow aspirate and trephine to characterise the plasma cell clone
Assessment of renal, hepatic and neurological organ involvement
redFlags: Advanced cardiac involvement with elevated biomarkers and heart failure
Syncope or arrhythmia suggesting cardiac amyloid
Rapidly progressive renal impairment or severe nephrotic syndrome
Bleeding tendency from factor X deficiency or vascular fragility
reference.prognosis: Prognosis is dominated by the extent of cardiac involvement; early diagnosis with limited cardiac disease allows good responses to plasma-cell-directed therapy, whereas advanced cardiac amyloidosis carries high early mortality.
pitfalls: Assuming amyloid found on biopsy is light-chain type without formal typing, risking wrong treatment
Missing the diagnosis in heart failure with preserved ejection fraction or non-diabetic proteinuria
Attributing a monoclonal protein to benign gammopathy while amyloid damages organs
Overlooking acquired bleeding risk before invasive procedures
management: Plasma-cell-directed therapy to suppress the amyloidogenic light chain, typically daratumumab combined with bortezomib, cyclophosphamide and dexamethasone
Autologous stem cell transplantation in carefully selected patients with limited cardiac involvement
Supportive treatment of restrictive cardiomyopathy with loop diuretics for congestion, avoiding agents poorly tolerated in infiltrative disease such as calcium channel blockers and digoxin
Management of nephrotic syndrome with diuretics, salt restriction and anti-proteinuric therapy
Monitor haematological response with serum free light chains and cardiac response with natriuretic peptides and troponin
Arrhythmia and conduction surveillance with anticoagulation given the thromboembolic risk of cardiac amyloidosis
Coordinate care through a specialist amyloidosis centre with haematology, cardiology and nephrology input
